decision_us: hard g, one syllable, rhymes with 'if' (/ɡɪf/)
alternative: soft g 'jif' (creator Steve Wilhite's / CompuServe spec's 'choosy programmers choose jif'); also letter-by-letter 'G-I-F' (common in China/Korea)
evidence: Stack Overflow 2017 dev survey (~64k devs): hard g 65.6%, soft g 26.3%, letters 6%, other 2%. Economist re-weighting by country population: hard 44% vs soft 32% vs letters 21%. Mashable 2013/14 (30,706 worldwide): ~70% hard g. eBay Deals US adults: 'gift'-style hard g ~54% vs 'jiff' 41%. Meyerweb (1,457 self-selected): hard 77.8%. Dictionaries: Merriam-Webster, Cambridge (US+UK show only /ɡɪf/), American Heritage list hard g first; Dictionary.com and Oxford Dictionary of English list soft first. Wilhite: 'It is a soft g... End of story.'

alternative: 'ping' (official per W3C PNG spec and libpng: 'PNG is pronounced ping')
evidence: No numeric poll found. Official spec (W3C, libpng) says 'ping', but Wiktionary lists letters first, and developer forum threads (GameDev.net 2013 'how do you pronounce your image formats', Wikipedia Talk:PNG) report overwhelmingly that people spell it out and many had never heard 'ping'; 'ping' also collides with the networking verb. Owner also says letters.

decision_us: letters 'S-Q-L' (/ˌɛs kjuː ˈɛl/) when standalone; dictation must accept both
alternative: 'sequel' (/ˈsiːkwəl/) — near-equal in usage, dominant in Microsoft/SQL Server and Oracle circles; dictation must map 'sequel' -> SQL in technical context
evidence: Evidence is essentially split. Hacker News 2010 poll: 'Sequel' 825 points vs 'S-Q-L' 766 (~52/48). ISO/ANSI standard and co-creator Don Chamberlin say 'ess-cue-ell'; Oracle docs say 'sequel'; MySQL docs say 'My Ess Que Ell'. Wiktionary lists letters first, 'sequel' second. Informal tally of ~20 database luminaries leaned 'sequel'. Tie broken toward letters by the standard, the creator, and the owner's own usage. No large modern survey exists.

MySQL reference manual: official pronunciation is 'My Ess Que Ell' (not 'my sequel'), though they 'do not mind' other pronunciations. Larry Ellison (Oracle, MySQL's owner) reportedly uses the official form. No poll; 'my sequel' is widely heard but the official form is well-established among practitioners.
D. Richard Hipp says pronounce it any way you like; he is heard saying 'Ess-Cue-El-ite' 'like a mineral'. Computer Hope gives ess-kue-ELL-ite. No poll; 'sequel-lite' common among sequel-sayers.

postgresql.org community survey (5,267 votes): post-gres-q-l 45.17%, post-gres 30.59%, postgres-sequel 10.90%, post-gree 6.65%, other <5%. Official FAQ: 'PostgreSQL is pronounced Post-Gres-Q-L... also shortened to Postgres, especially in conversation.'
Official FAQ endorses 'Postgres' as the conversational short form; 30.59% of 5,267 survey voters said they use 'post-gres' for PostgreSQL itself.

Strong practitioner convention: the Microsoft ecosystem overwhelmingly says 'sequel server' (LearnSQL, TablePlus/StackExchange norm, Microsoft webcasts; even Larry Ellison says 'Microsoft SEQUEL Server'). Exception to the standalone-SQL rule: in this product name, use 'sequel'.

alternative: 'weppy' (/ˈwɛpi/, Google's 2010 launch page: 'Did you know? WebP is pronounced weppy'; note removed by ~2012)
evidence: No poll exists. Google's original guidance was 'weppy', but the note disappeared from Google's site by 2012 and forum users report never having heard 'weppy' (Realmac forum, Lemmy threads); spelled-out 'web-P' is the form heard in practice. TechTerms still lists 'weppy'. Owner says 'web-P'.
Cambridge (UK & US) /ˈdʒeɪ.peɡ/; Wiktionary same for RP/GenAm/CanE. Undisputed in practice.
JPG is just the 3-letter extension of JPEG; practitioners read it as 'JAY-peg'. Letter-by-letter 'J-P-G' is heard when distinguishing the extension. No poll.

No survey. comp.lang.c FAQ: char/care/car all acceptable, 'the choice is arbitrary'. Jargon File: /keir/ or /char/ usual, /kar/ rarer. Stroustrup's C++ FAQ (as quoted): usually pronounced 'tchar', not 'kar'. Student/teacher threads (Treehouse) report instructors mostly saying 'char'.

alternative: 'LYE-nucks' (/ˈlaɪnəks/, listed by Cambridge UK as a variant); 'LEE-nooks' (Torvalds' original Swedish-influenced form)
evidence: Cambridge US /ˈlɪn.əks/ (UK also /ˈlɪn.əks/, with /ˈlaɪnəks/ variant). Wiktionary /ˈlɪnəks/, /ˈlɪnʊks/. Torvalds' kernel.org 'how to pronounce Linux' recording uses a short i. Universal in practice.

No poll found. Kubernetes 1.9 CHANGELOG: 'The canonical pronunciation of kubectl is "cube control"'; Kelsey Hightower and many maintainers say 'koob-control'. Community collection (saada/kubectl-pronounciation) lists cube-control, cube-C-T-L, cube-cuddle; DevOpsDays talk 'Pronouncing kubectl: The Definitive Guide' shows no consensus. 'Kube' vowel matches Kubernetes (/kuː/), though 'cube' (/kjuː/) is also common.
Wiktionary /k(j)uːbəˈnɛtɪs/, /-ˈneɪtiːz/; Blue Matador and most conference talks: coo-ber-net-ees. Greek κυβερνήτης origin. Practitioner consensus.
GitLab and dev.to explainers: K8s is pronounced 'Kates'; Brendan Burns (co-creator) reported that the team says either 'kubernetes' or 'k-eights'. Blue Matador advises against 'k-eights'. No poll.
Official: 'NGINX (pronounced "engine x")' on nginx.com; Wikipedia IPA /ˌɛndʒɪnˈɛks/. Practitioners overwhelmingly follow the official form.

alternative: 'SOO-doh' (homophone of 'pseudo'), acknowledged as common by the maintainer
evidence: Maintainer Todd C. Miller: 'The correct pronunciation is sue due / soo doo for superuser do'; sudo.ws troubleshooting: official 'soo-doo', 'pseudo' homophone also common. Wiktionary lists 'soo-doo' first and tags 'soo-doh' as a spelling pronunciation. No poll; both widely heard.

No poll found. Wiktionary lists hard g /ˈɹɛɡɛks/ first, soft /ˈɹɛdʒɛks/ second; a 2018 Medium post says hard g is 'the more common'. Both are heavily used; soft g is very common in spoken US usage, so dictation must accept both.

alternative: 'TOR-ee'; Latin/astronomy 'TOR-eye' (genitive of Taurus, as in Alpha Tauri)
evidence: No official pronunciation in Tauri docs, GitHub, or trademark guidelines (searched). Name evokes Latin Tauri / the Tauri people; Latin-dictionary reading is 'TOR-eye' but the developer community typically says 'TOW-ree' / 'TOR-ee'. Needs owner confirmation.
Official spec abstract (yaml.org 1.0 through 1.2.2): 'YAML (rhymes with "camel")'. Wiktionary /ˈjæməl/. Undisputed.

alternative: 'JAY-sahn' (/ˈdʒeɪˌsɑn/, stressed 'son' syllable — very common among US developers)
evidence: ECMA-404 2nd ed. / ISO/IEC 21778:2017 assign the 'Jason' pronunciation; Crockford: 'I strictly don't care'. Wiktionary GA lists /ˈdʒeɪsən/ first, /ˈdʒeɪˌsɑn/ second. UNIX & Linux System Administration Handbook says 'JAY-sawn seems to have become more common'. No poll; near-split in US practice.
Cambridge UK & US: /ˈɡuː.i/ only. Wiktionary lists both. Practitioner standard.
Cambridge UK & US: /ˌjuː.ɑːrˈel/. Wiktionary tags 'earl' as rare (used by some early web pioneers).
No dictionary or poll; spelled-out form is standard in docs, talks and tutorials (e.g., 'the AWS C-L-I'). Acronym readings are rare.
Cambridge UK & US /ˈæs.ki/; Wiktionary /ˈæski/. Undisputed.

Cambridge US /ˈæʒ.ɚ/, UK /ˈæʒ.ər/ (also /ˈæz.jʊər/). Wiktionary lists /ˈæʒə/ first for UK and /ˈæʒɚ/ for US. Microsoft's #HowISayAzure (2021) campaign embraced variation; Satya Nadella and Scott Guthrie say roughly 'AZH-er'.
Cambridge UK /ˈdeɪ.tə/, US /ˈdeɪ.t̬ə/ first (then /ˈdæt̬ə/, /ˈdɑt̬ə/). Wiktionary lists /ˈdeɪtə/ for RP and GA.
Cambridge UK & US /kæʃ/ only; Wiktionary marks /kæˈʃeɪ/ proscribed.
Cambridge US /ˈraʊ.t̬ɚ/ (and /ˈruːtər/ as a variant); Wiktionary: GA /ˈɹaʊtɚ/, RP /ˈɹuːtə/ for the networking device. Classic US/UK split.

alternative: 'JIG-uh-byte' (older US variant, cf. 'jigawatts' in Back to the Future)
evidence: Cambridge UK & US /ˈɡɪɡ.ə.baɪt/ only; Wiktionary US lists hard g first, /ˈdʒɪɡə-/ second.

Huawei's own 2012 and 2015 New York pronunciation campaigns taught 'WAH-way' (Android Central, PhoneArena, Macworld). Wiktionary gives /ˈhwɑːweɪ/ and marks 'wah-way' as proscribed vs Mandarin, but 'WAH-way' is the company-taught and widely used English form.
Hugo Barra (then Xiaomi VP) on video: 'show-me', with 'show' as in 'shower' (Mandarin xiǎo mǐ, 'little rice').

Wiktionary English 'mistral' (the wind) /mɪˈstɹɑːl/; company is French [mistʁal]. English-speaking practitioners and podcasts mostly follow the second-syllable stress; 'MIS-trul' heard but less common. No poll.
Plain English words; company named after the 🤗 emoji. No dispute.

Qwen Technical Report (Alibaba, arXiv 2309.16609): pronunciation 'can vary... one possible way to pronounce it: /kwɛn/'. English-speaking practitioners mostly say 'kwen'; 'chwen' advocated as closer to the pinyin of Tongyi Qianwen. No poll.
Plain English compound; universal.
Standard English adjective 'anthropic' (as in 'anthropic principle'), stress on second syllable; used by company leadership in interviews.
Nvidia brand guidelines: 'en-VID-ee-uh' (Fortune, Business Insider). From Latin invidia (envy).
Grafana community forum: 'Grah-fah-nah', pointing to CEO Raj Dutt and creator Torkel Ödegaard saying it at the GrafanaCon 2016 kickoff; stress on the second syllable in their talks. No poll.
Wikipedia IPA /ˈrɛdɪs/ (from REmote DIctionary Server). No reliable source for 'REE-dis'.
Official README: 'Deno (/ˈdiːnoʊ/, pronounced dee-no)'; Ryan Dahl uses it; dinosaur mascot reinforces it. 'DEN-oh' heard among newcomers. No poll.
Official README/guide: 'Vite (French word for "quick", pronounced /viːt/, like "veet")' with an audio link; Evan You and ViteConf use it.
Plain English word (bun.sh). No dispute.

alternative: 'AV-uh-neer' (anglicised first-syllable stress, common among US designers)
evidence: Typeface by Adrian Frutiger (Linotype, 1988); name is French avenir 'future' [av.niʁ]. No poll or foundry pronunciation guide found; both forms common in design circles.
Wiktionary 'Bézier curve' /ˈbɛz.i.eɪ/; Merriam-Webster has an entry for Bezier curve. French original [bezje]. Designers and graphics engineers overwhelmingly say 'BEZ-ee-ay'.
AAII financial dictionary: 'ee-bit-dah'; Wiktionary lists /iːbɪtˈdɑː/ first; Fishbowl finance threads show 'EE-BIT-DAH' as the majority with 'EH-bit-dah' variants. Cambridge (UK) gives /ˈebɪtdə/.
Wiktionary lists both (/ˌɛsˌkeɪˈjuː/ and /skjuː/). In retail/e-commerce/product practice 'skew' is the dominant spoken form; letters common in some enterprise/UK settings. No poll.
Marc Randolph's Netflix memoir 'That Will Never Work': 'Pronounced kack, it stands for cost of acquiring a customer.' Common in SaaS/VC talk ('CAC payback'). No poll.
No dictionary pronunciation found (Wiktionary defines only). Telecom/SaaS practitioners commonly say 'AR-poo' in earnings calls; letters also heard. Low evidence.
Heroku's own About page (archived) gave 'her-OH-koo'; name is a portmanteau of 'heroic' + 'haiku'.
No official guide found; name derived from 'calendar' + '-ly', and the stress pattern 'kuh-LEND-lee' is what the company's founder and users say in videos. Low dispute in practice.
Zapier's own slogan/community: 'Zapier makes you happier' — rhymes with happier.
Asana About page: 'We typically pronounce Asana with the emphasis on the second syllable: uh-sāh-nuh', while accepting the Sanskrit 'āh-suh-nuh'. Asana staff on forum: 'ah-SAH-na'.
Plain English compound (Figma's whiteboard). No dispute.
Named after painter Joan Miró (CEO Andrey Khusid, Intercom interview). Miro community accepted answer: 'Mee-ro', per official YouTube channel; 'My-ro' heard among new users.
